task_question: Does the evidence support dual-process theory (System 1/System 2) as distinct cognitive systems, or as a continuum of processing?

evidence_items.content: Kahneman (2011) presents extensive behavioral evidence for two distinct modes of thinking: fast/intuitive (System 1) and slow/deliberative (System 2). Response time data shows bimodal distributions on conjunction fallacy tasks.

Neuroimaging meta-analysis (Goel, 2007) shows overlapping activation patterns for intuitive and deliberative reasoning, with no clear anatomical boundary between proposed System 1 and System 2 regions.
Melnikoff & Bargh (2018) argue that dual-process theories are unfalsifiable as stated, and that cognitive control exists on a continuum of automaticity.
evidence_items.source: Melnikoff & Bargh, Trends in Cognitive Sciences

evidence_items.content: De Neys (2021) proposes an integrative model where logical intuitions and heuristic intuitions compete, preserving the phenomenology of dual processing without requiring discrete systems.
evidence_items.source: De Neys, Perspectives on Psychological Science

evidence_items.content: A news article claims 'Scientists prove brain has two distinct thinking systems' based on a single fMRI study with N=12.
evidence_items.source: Science Daily rewrite of preliminary study

evidence_items.content: General educational psychology textbook repeats the dual-process framework as established fact, citing only Kahneman.
Recent computational modeling shows that a single neural network can exhibit both fast/automatic and slow/controlled processing modes depending on task demands and training, without separate systems.
